summary: For ages 12–14, teaches reconstructing an ancient ecosystem by synthesising multiple independent lines of fossil evidence: tooth isotopes (oxygen for seasonal climate/water source and, compared with local baselines, possible movement; carbon for diet type), bone histology growth rings (age-at-death and growth rate), coprolite contents/chemistry (diet), and fossil plant assemblages (habitat/climate). The central skill is triangulation — any one proxy is partial; combining independent lines yields a cross-checked picture, agreement raises confidence, and a conflict between proxies is itself an informative clue to investigate, not necessarily a mistake.
misconceptions: 'Bones alone tell the whole story' — diet, migration, age and habitat come from other proxies (isotopes, histology, coprolites, plants).
'One line of evidence is enough' — robust reconstructions triangulate multiple independent sources.
'Conflicting evidence means someone made a mistake' — a clash can reveal something real (e.g. dietary change, reworking).
'Palaeontology is just digging up bones' — it is a lab-based, multidisciplinary evidence science.
'Growth rings/isotopes give exact answers' — they give constrained estimates with uncertainty.

activities.title: The palaeo-lab: reconstruct one mystery animal from four proxies
steps: Work through a multi-station lab investigating a single mystery animal: (1) section a leg bone and count the growth rings to estimate age-at-death and whether it was still growing fast when it died; (2) read a tooth's isotope trace along the crown — a seasonal rhythm in oxygen (δ18O) records seasonal changes in drinking water and climate, which even an animal that never moves will show; movement between regions (migration) is suggested only when values shift away from the local baseline, ideally checked with another tracer such as strontium; carbon (δ13C) indicates diet type (e.g. C4 grassland grazing vs C3 browsing where C4 grasses existed, or open vs closed-canopy feeding); (3) examine a coprolite linked to the animal (by size, shape and where it was found, which is itself an inference) and identify plant or bone fragments to establish diet; (4) identify a fossil leaf assemblage to reconstruct habitat and climate.
Record a distinct inference from each station rather than one overall guess.
Combine the separate results into a single ecosystem reconstruction (diet, age/growth, seasonal movement, habitat), stating which evidence supports each claim.

Encounter a built-in case where two proxies appear to conflict, and decide how to interpret the clash (e.g. a genuine dietary change over the animal's life, seasonal variation, or reworked material) rather than discarding one result.

Rate which conclusions are strongest and explain why — those where independent lines converge are more reliable than those resting on a single ambiguous source. Treat each proxy's answer as a constrained estimate with uncertainty, not an exact value.
activities.insight: Robust reconstructions come from triangulating multiple independent proxies: each proxy answers a specific question, convergence builds justified confidence, and a conflict is a clue worth investigating.

activities.title: Match the proxy to the inference
steps: Match each proxy to the inference it supports: growth rings ↔ age and growth rate; tooth δ18O ↔ seasonal climate/water source (possible migration only if values depart from the local baseline); tooth δ18O ↔ diet type is wrong, so pair tooth δ13C ↔ diet type; coprolite contents ↔ diet; fossil plant assemblage ↔ habitat/climate.
Sequence the analysis workflow for investigating a specimen.
Answer why combining several independent lines is stronger than relying on one.
activities.insight: Knowing which method answers which question, and why multiple lines beat a single source, underpins being able to perform the synthesis.

activities.title: Guided tour of a reconstructed ecosystem scene
steps: Explore an annotated reconstructed-ecosystem scene with tap-to-reveal 'how we know' tags: tapping an animal or plant reveals which proxy and analysis established each fact.
After exploring, name two kinds of evidence beyond bones and what each tells you, then explain how growth rings or tooth isotopes are read for one specific inference.
activities.insight: Many facts about a vanished ecosystem are established by specific analytical methods, not by bones alone.

activities.title: Ask a palaeoecologist: how do a tooth and a fossilised dropping tell the same story?
steps: Pose questions to a (simulated or role-played) researcher, e.g. 'How do a tooth and a fossilised dropping end up telling the same story?' and 'What do you do when two techniques disagree?'
Summarise in your own words how disparate techniques are combined into one reconstruction and why agreement across them matters.
activities.insight: Palaeontology is a modern, multidisciplinary lab science (chemistry, histology, botany) that weaves faint, independent threads of evidence into one testable picture.

checkQuestion: Here is an evidence dossier for one dinosaur and its rock formation: a tooth with its oxygen-isotope ratios measured at different growth stages, a thin cross-section of a leg bone showing rings, a coprolite, and a list of fossil plants found in the same rock. Using these, reconstruct as much as you can about this animal's life and its ecosystem — diet, growth and age, any seasonal movement, and habitat — and for each claim state which evidence supports it. Then tell me which conclusions are strongest and why.
checkAnswer: Oxygen-isotope shifts along the tooth indicate the animal moved between locations across seasons (migration); bone growth rings give growth rate and approximate age at death; the coprolite's contents indicate diet; the fossil plant assemblage indicates the habitat. The strongest conclusions are those where independent lines converge (e.g. coprolite diet agreeing with the plant assemblage); each single source alone is weaker, so the richest, most reliable picture comes from synthesising them.
